analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income and estate taxes with a simplified three-bracket tax, refundable family and work credits, and new business tax rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with zero cosponsors, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the entire federal income tax system — including the corporate tax, the alternative minimum tax, and the estate and gift tax — and replaced it with a single "Simplified USA Tax" with two parts: a tax on individuals at three rates (15%, 25%, 30%) and a tax on business profits. It would keep deductions for mortgage interest, charity, and college costs, add a refundable credit for every family, a refundable credit for low-wage workers, and a refundable credit refunding Social Security payroll taxes, and let anyone contribute to a Roth IRA. Businesses would pay 8% on their first $150,000 of profit and 12% above that, write off equipment purchases immediately, and pay no tax at all on export or other foreign-source income, while imports would be taxed. The estate and gift tax would be repealed outright.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed: low- and moderate-wage workers, through a refundable family credit of up to $3,300 for joint filers plus $1,500 per child, a work credit worth up to 40% of earnings for parents, and a full refund of the employee share of Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes. Households would also get a simpler return described as a small fraction of the current Form 1040. At the other end, the wealthiest households would benefit from permanent repeal of the estate and gift tax, and investors from a 15% ceiling on tax on dividends and capital gains. Exporting and multinational businesses would pay no tax on export or foreign-source income; all businesses would get immediate expensing of equipment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers, families, large estates, exporters

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable family tax credit — $3,300 for a married couple filing jointly, $2,800 for an unmarried parent, $1,150 per dependent, plus $1,500 for each qualifying child — that reduces tax even below zero as a refund.

Creates a refundable work tax credit worth 34% of earnings for one-child families and 40% for families with two or more children, up to dollar caps, phasing out above roughly $17,000–$21,000 of income.

Allows every worker a refundable credit equal to the employee share of Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, so the payroll tax no longer falls entirely on income tax returns' bottom line; the bill states this does not reduce Social Security trust fund balances or benefits.

Replaces the current return with a tax the bill describes as reportable on a form 'only a small fraction the size of Form 1040', with far fewer deductions and credits, and repeals the individual and corporate alternative minimum tax.

Cuts the tax on business profits to 8% on the first $150,000 and 12% above that, lets businesses expense (immediately deduct) the cost of plant and equipment instead of depreciating it, and exempts export sales income and other foreign-source income from tax while taxing imports.
Repeals the estate and gift tax entirely, and repeals the individual and corporate income tax structure in favor of a single integrated tax.
Caps the tax rate on net investment income — dividends and gains on asset sales — at 15%, regardless of how high a filer's other income is.

analysis.who_pays: The bill's own statement that businesses and individuals would keep paying 'about the same portion of the total tax' depended on rate and base choices a full revenue analysis never performed, since the bill never advanced. Workers would lose tax-free treatment of several employer-provided fringe benefits — employer-paid parking, educational benefits, meals, housing, group legal plans, and dependent care assistance would all count as taxable income under the bill's gross-income rules. The federal government would permanently give up estate and gift tax revenue and the current corporate tax base, shifting whatever shortfall resulted onto the remaining taxpayers or borrowing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fringe-benefit recipients; remaining taxpayers via revenue loss

drawbacks.text: Permanent repeal of the estate and gift tax would eliminate the only federal tax on very large inherited fortunes, and the bill caps tax on investment income at 15% — both provisions direct their largest benefits to the wealthiest households.

Exempting all export sales income and other foreign-source income from business tax while taxing imports would shrink the business tax base substantially and concentrate the benefit on multinational and export-oriented firms.

The bill taxes several employer-provided fringe benefits as income — including employer-paid parking, education benefits, meals, housing, and dependent care assistance — which would raise taxes on some workers even as other credits lower them.

Replacing the entire income, corporate, and estate tax system in a single stroke for years after 2006 was a sweeping change with no committee analysis, hearing, or revenue estimate ever performed on this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill genuinely mixed the two stories. Its refundable family, work, and payroll-tax credits would have made the tax system meaningfully more generous to low-wage working families and eliminated the payroll tax as a net burden on the poor, and its simplification promises were real. But its business and wealth-side provisions — full estate tax repeal, a 15% ceiling on investment income, and untaxed export and foreign income — directed large, permanent benefits to the wealthiest households and multinational firms, and its fringe-benefit taxation would have raised taxes on some ordinary workers. With zero cosponsors and no committee action, no revenue estimate or distributional analysis ever tested whether the credits would have survived contact with the arithmetic.

outcome.mechanism: A single House member introduced the bill, the Ways and Means Committee sat on it with no hearing or markup, no other member signed on, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil English (R-PA) introduced the Simplified USA Tax Act of 2006 in the House on February 8, 2006.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and no further action of any kind appears in its history — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without the bill ever leaving committee; bills that die at the end of a Congress must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position because nothing happened: every household and business kept paying tax under the existing code, so the current beneficiaries of tax preferences — including estates exempt from the estate tax as it then stood, and industries with existing deductions — kept what they had. Committee leaders were spared having to schedule a vote on a tax-system rewrite with no support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; existing tax rules stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.role: Sponsor; Member of the House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors and was never voted on, so the record shows no partisan split — only a lone Republican sponsor and an unresponsive committee.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift tax outright and caps the tax on dividends and capital gains at 15%, provisions whose value rises with the size of the estate or portfolio. Their cost is borne by whatever revenue replaces it.

Export sales income and other foreign-source income would be exempt from business tax entirely, while imports would be taxed — a large benefit concentrated in internationally active firms. Some of it could flow to domestic workers through export competitiveness, but the direct gain goes to the firms.

The 15% ceiling on investment income and vastly expanded Roth IRA eligibility (anyone could contribute up to their full income, with tax-free withdrawals after five years) would channel more money through investment accounts and cut taxes on fund returns.

An 8% rate on the first $150,000 of business profit and immediate expensing of equipment would cut taxes for most businesses that owe tax under the current corporate structure. The bill states the business share of total tax would stay roughly the same overall.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and the housing market
industries.note: The bill preserves a homeowner deduction for mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to $1,000,000, keeping the existing tax advantage of borrowed home ownership in place.
A philanthropic transfer deduction survives (up to 50% of income for regular charities), preserving the tax incentive for charitable giving that supports nonprofit revenue.
A new education deduction of up to $4,000 per student and $12,000 per return for tuition and fees would subsidize families paying college costs.

The bill's stated goal is a return 'only a small fraction the size of Form 1040' with few deductions and credits, which would reduce the demand for paid preparers and complex filing software that the current code supports.

Businesses would gain from lower rates and expensing, but employer-paid fringe benefits — parking, education, meals, housing, group legal plans, dependent care — would become taxable income to employees, reducing the value of compensation packages built on those benefits.
